newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China hands hijack suspect to Taiwan authorities.
newsitem.headline: China hands hijack suspect to Taiwan authorities.

text.p: Taiwan authorities sailed directly to the Chinese mainland on Wednesday and took custody of an accused hijacker who faces trial on the island, completing a rare cooperative exchange with its communist arch rival.

"We have received the hijacker," Lin Ching-ping, deputy secretary-general of Taiwan's quasi-official Straits Exchange Foundation, told Reuters by telephone after Liu Shan-chung's handover in the mainland port city of Xiamen.

Liu was taken aboard a Taiwan fishing boat for a short sail to the Taiwan-held island of Quemoy, also known as Jinmen, a few kilometres (miles) from Xiamen and would be put aboard a plane for the half-hour flight to Taipei, Lin said.

Officials of the Taiwan foundation, accompanied by police and advisers from the cabinet's policy-making Mainland Affairs Council, went briefly ashore in Xiamen and signed documents taking custody of Liu. Officials of Beijing's state-sanctioned Red Cross signed for the mainland, Lin said.

Liu, an unemployed reporter, is accused of commandeering a Taiwan commercial jet to Xiamen on March 10, becoming the first hijacker in the 1990s to force a passenger plane from the island to the mainland rather than the other way around.

His transfer marked the first hijacker repatriation between Taiwan and the mainland. It was completed even though a repatriation pact negotiated in 1995 has never been signed due to subsequent political tensions.

The transfer also came despite a freeze in quasi-official bilateral contacts dating to June 1995, when Beijing ended what had been gradually warming talks in an angry response to a controversial U.S. visit by Taiwan President Lee Teng-hui.
Taiwan and China have had no formal contacts since a civil war split them in 1949. Beijing regards the Nationalist-ruled island as a renegade province.
